crime.value: Two killings: teenager Richard Gorman stabs his mother's lover Laramer ~32 times with an icepick, then later stabs his mother to death during a sanitarium visit. The question is not whodunit (he confesses immediately) but why — what psychological mechanism drove him to act.
crime.quote: “I’m Richard Gorman, sir,’ he said. ‘I just killed a man.’”

victim.value: Laramer, a drunken, brutal live-in lover of Gorman's widowed mother who beat the boy and displaced him; later Mrs. Gorman herself, a promiscuous, neglectful mother whose 'dishonor' made her the target of the Orestes-pattern killing
victim.quote: “he was a lush, a drunken bum and he started beating hell out of me all the time, but she didn’t care”

closed_world.value: The institutional circuit of Juvenile Detention, jail, the Lunacy Commission, and finally the enclosed grounds of Green Valley Manor private sanitarium — a controlled therapeutic world Kessler himself designed
closed_world.quote: “Green Valley Manor resembled a lovely lakeside resort. Parklike grounds contained numerous small cottages”

culprit_and_motive.value: Gorman is the literal killer, but the true culprit is Dr. Kessler, whose psychoanalytic tutoring and reading list (Hamlet, Oedipus, Orestes) supplied Gorman a mythic script; Kessler's own repressed hatred of women steered the boy to matricide — he is Apollo, who commanded Orestes to kill his mother
culprit_and_motive.quote: “I hated her too, he thought. I always hated women.”

resolution.value: No legal restoration; instead a psychological revelation — Kessler discovers the second corpse and recognizes his own complicity, whispering 'my name is Apollo.' Order is not restored, it collapses.
resolution.quote: “he whispered, ‘Look at me, Richard. Look at me—don’t you know—my name is Apollo. . .’”

investigator.value: Dr. Kessler, senior psychiatrist and head of the Mental Hygiene Clinic — an outsider to police work who investigates motive rather than identity, and is ultimately revealed as the unwitting instigator
investigator.quote: “Mine can only begin now, because I’m interested in why he did it.”

suspect_architecture.value: Not a whodunit: the killer (Richard Gorman) is known and confessed from the first page. The 'cast' consists of Gorman, his psychiatrist Kessler, Lt. Reed, and Mrs. Gorman as victim-to-be; differentiation is by interpretive stance (police 'simple revenge' vs. psychiatric 'complex') rather than by means/motive/opportunity.
suspect_architecture.quote: “The kid confessed,” Lt. Reed said. “What else is there to know?”

red_herring.value: The Oedipus complex diagnosis itself is the planted false trail — Kessler's Hamlet/patricide framework misdirects both doctor and reader from the mother-directed Orestes pattern; Gorman's gentle record and lack of delinquency reinforce the misreading.
red_herring.quote: “The classical Oedipus complex. Just remember the dynamics of the complex.”

clue_fairness.value: Fairly clued: the reader sees Gorman identify with Hamlet rather than Oedipus, fixate on the Closet Scene, quote Orestes ('thy sin destroyeth thee'), and ask to see his mother — all before the second murder.
clue_fairness.quote: Gorman identified himself with Hamlet, rather than with Oedipus, and seemed especially intrigued by the Closet Scene.

social_world.value: Institutional power map of psychiatry vs. law enforcement: police/D.A. want a hanging, the Lunacy Commission decides sanity, and Kessler's patronage — he co-founded Green Valley Manor and can admit charity cases — lets him move a killer from asylum to private cottage.
social_world.quote: a private sanitarium known as Green Valley Manor on which Kessler served as a part-time resident staff member

alibi.value: No alibi element; Gorman never denies or conceals — he walks up to a patrolman with the bloody icepick and confesses immediately.
alibi.quote: “I’m Richard Gorman, sir,” he said. “I just killed a man.”

reveal_mechanic.value: Psychological demonstration: Gorman explains the corrected 'Orestes complex' aloud, Kessler runs to the cottage and finds Mrs. Gorman stabbed dead, and the final proof lands when Kessler recalls that it was Apollo who commanded Orestes to kill his mother — making the analyst the instigator.
reveal_mechanic.quote: “Look at me, Richard. Look at me—don’t you know—my name is Apollo. . .”

media_and_audience.value: The crime is packaged by newspapers, police contempt ('punk', 'floozie'), neighbours' and employer's testimony to Gorman's sweetness, and above all by the legal theatre of the Lunacy Commission, which Kessler wins with jargon he privately calls 'canned language'.
media_and_audience.quote: It was very necessary if you were to impress the Lunacy Commission.

investigator_wound.value: Kessler's own unexamined misogyny — a divorced man with 'hostility toward women' who kept Mrs. Gorman out of the analysis, thereby steering his patient toward matricide and discovering his own hatred in the moment of horror.
investigator_wound.quote: And then Kessler knew. I hated her too, he thought. I always hated women.

victims_enemies.value: Laramer, the mother's live-in lover, was hated by the boy he beat, evicted, and displaced; he also beat Mrs. Gorman, and lived off the boy's factory pay. Later Mrs. Gorman herself becomes a victim, hated by her son for neglect and promiscuity — and, it emerges, quietly loathed by Kessler too.
victims_enemies.quote: he started kicking me out of my own house and beating hell out of me. . .and he hit her too

suspect_wounds.value: Gorman's wound is not that he looks guilty — he confesses — but that his 'normal, well-behaved kid' record makes his guilt unbelievable. Kessler's own wound is his unexamined hostility toward women, which he suppresses and which shapes his misdiagnosis.
suspect_wounds.quote: Self-analytical work, however, seemed to reveal deeper motives, certain suggestions of hostility toward women.

unreliable_frame.value: The story is filtered through Kessler's clinical self-assurance; he believes he is objective while steering Gorman toward a preordained Oedipal reading and deliberately excluding the mother from analysis. Gorman in turn parrots back whatever framework he is given, so his 'insights' are Kessler's own words returned.
unreliable_frame.quote: he had been carefully keeping Mrs. Gorman out of this psychoanalytical process as much as possible

setting_as_constraint.value: Institutional custody defines every possibility: jail, Juvenile Detention, then the asylum. Green Valley Manor's private cottages and unsupervised 5-to-7 visiting hours — a resort-like sanitarium Kessler himself helped found — created the sealed, permissive space in which Gorman could be alone with his mother.
setting_as_constraint.quote: "Visiting hours are from five to seven. You can entertain her here in your private cottage."

evidence_type.value: Testimonial and documentary — the recorded interviews, psychological tests, and Kessler's voluminous brief. Ultimately literary evidence: Gorman's shift from identifying with Hamlet's Closet Scene to quoting Orestes ('Thy sin destroyeth thee') is the clue that predicts the second murder.
evidence_type.quote: The small note recorder in Kessler's pocket faithfully preserved Gorman's testimony.

false_suspect.value: No conventional false suspect; guilt is admitted at once. The displaced 'culprit' is Laramer as father-substitute — the mother's true role as target being concealed until the end, and Kessler being the unrecognized instigator, the Apollo who commanded the matricide.
false_suspect.quote: he remembered who it had been who told the young noble Orestes to kill his mother

technical_detail.value: Psychoanalytic and legal-psychiatric technique: the Oedipus complex, irresistible impulse, and the right/wrong test of legal insanity — plus the therapeutic use of prescribed literature (Hamlet, Sophocles, Orestes), which supplies the patient with both a diagnosis and a script for the next killing.
technical_detail.quote: he believed in giving a patient literature that seemed to have a special application to his problem

moral_ambiguity.value: Kessler acts throughout from genuine compassion and scientific curiosity, saving a boy from the gallows and giving him literacy and selfhood; yet his vanity, his blind spot about women, and his prescriptive reading list make him the author of the second murder. Gorman kills believing himself cured and obedient, radiant rather than malevolent.
moral_ambiguity.quote: "I'm really well now, really purged. It wasn't complete, sir, before."
